title: {{NAME}} and the Volcano That the Algorithm Forgot
moral: The bravest heroes are the ones who ask for help when they need it most.

pages.content:
Mount Craterhorn had been sleeping for six hundred years, which was precisely the problem. Everything that had been built near it, the gleaming Jurassic Research Station, the valley villages, the migration paths of three separate dinosaur herds, all of it relied on the mountain staying asleep. And when AXIOM-7, the volcano-monitoring robot, marched into the station with steam venting from every joint and announced that his seismic sensors had detected something the algorithm classified as 'impossible,' the whole valley went very, very quiet.

{{NAME}} had been refuelling at the station after a routine patrol when AXIOM-7's red alert light began spinning. The robot was enormous, built like a refrigerator stacked atop another refrigerator, with a round sensor-dome for a head and six articulated arms for collecting geological samples. Right now, all six arms were gesturing simultaneously, which was AXIOM-7's version of shouting.

Outside the panoramic window, three herds of Brachiosaurus were raising their long necks toward the mountain with an expression {{NAME}} recognised from years of flying patrol. It was not curiosity. It was the ancient animal knowledge of something wrong. The ground gave a single, low shudder, like a sleeping giant rolling over. Then it was still. The stillness was worse.

pages.content:
AXIOM-7 laid out the data on the holographic display with the crisp precision of a machine that had never once been wrong. The seismic signature didn't match any known eruption pattern. It matched something older, a deep geological fault line that the original survey maps, drawn before AXIOM-7's construction, had simply missed. The algorithm hadn't factored it in because it didn't know it existed.

'The migration routes,' {{NAME}} said, pressing a finger to the map. 'If the three herds go north as programmed, they'll be directly in the ash zone.' AXIOM-7's sensor dome rotated with a soft whir. 'Confirmed. Re-routing requires manual coordination. My movement algorithms are calibrated for survey work, not herding. I cannot do this alone.'

The admission cost the robot something. {{NAME}} could tell by the way AXIOM-7's posture shifted, the arms folding inward slightly, the sensor light dimming to a cooler blue. For a machine built to be comprehensive, perfect, and self-sufficient, saying 'I cannot do this alone' was not in any original programming. It had been learned.

{{NAME}}'s mask dropped to full position with a satisfying click. 'Good,' said {{NAME}} simply. 'Neither can I.' AXIOM-7's light brightened to warm gold. Something passed between them in that moment, a current of understanding that had nothing to do with volcanoes.

pages.content:
The next thirty minutes were the fastest and noisiest of {{NAME}}'s life.

AXIOM-7 fired signal flares from all six arms simultaneously, painting the sky in crackling blue and gold arcs that sent the nearest Brachiosaurus herd lurching westward in alarm. {{NAME}} flew ahead of the second herd at full speed, cobalt cape snapping like a flag in a gale, using every trick learned in three years of aerial patrol: banking sharp, calling loud, pushing the air ahead like a bow wave. Dinosaurs are not fast to turn. They are, however, responsive to a small determined figure appearing directly in their path and waving vigorously.

The third herd was the problem. They were heading north with the calm, implacable certainty of creatures who had walked the same path for ten thousand years. Nothing had ever made them change it. They were not going to start for a robot and a child.

But the lead Brachiosaurus, a colossal matriarch whose neck reached forty feet into the afternoon sky, paused. AXIOM-7 had sent a low-frequency signal, the precise vibration the geological record showed had preceded the last ice age. The one all living things carried as a memory in their deepest instincts. The matriarch swung her long neck west. The herd followed. Every single one.

pages.content:
Mount Craterhorn erupted at exactly 4:47 in the afternoon, which AXIOM-7 logged with mechanical precision and {{NAME}} experienced as the sky turning orange and the ground punching upward through the soles of both boots.

A column of ash and steam billowed miles into the air, catching the sunlight and scattering it into apocalyptic amber. The north valley, the place the three herds would have been, vanished behind a curtain of falling rock and slow, magnificent lava. But the herds were west. Safe in the broad clearing beyond the ridge, all three groups milling together with the slightly bewildered energy of strangers thrown into the same room by weather.

{{NAME}} landed on a boulder and watched Craterhorn perform its ancient, impossible spectacle. AXIOM-7 landed beside with a controlled thud of six hundred kilograms of robot and surveyed the eruption through every sensor simultaneously. 'All three herds: confirmed safe,' he announced. His voice modulator, which was calibrated for data delivery rather than emotion, managed to sound something very close to moved.

{{NAME}} sat on the boulder with the ash falling like warm grey snow and felt the particular quiet that comes after a very large thing is done. Craterhorn roared into the sunset. It was extraordinary and terrible and beautiful all at once.

pages.content:
The herds were reunited by nightfall. The lead matriarch and the other group leaders stood neck-to-neck in the clearing, a huddle of ancient giants touching foreheads in a way that seemed, if you were watching carefully, like conversation.

AXIOM-7 ran seventeen separate post-event calculations and then did something no one had programmed him to do. He sat down. Not for maintenance. Not for a recharge. He simply sat beside {{NAME}} on the warm hillside and watched the dinosaurs, and his sensor dome made a slow, contented rotation.

'You could have deployed without me,' {{NAME}} said. 'Once the herds were moving, you had enough data.' AXIOM-7's light pulsed gently. 'The data was sufficient. The experience was better shared.' He paused, all six arms still. 'I will update my operational parameters.'

The new stars were arriving, one by one, like small ideas becoming large ones. {{NAME}} leaned against the warm metal of AXIOM-7's side, which conducted heat surprisingly well, and felt the long slow breathing of the world settling back into its rhythms. Sleep now, little hero. Let your muscles unknot themselves and your thoughts go soft and slow. And tomorrow, when the valley is clear and green again, look up. Because the matriarch Brachiosaurus has a calf that no survey has yet recorded, and it is doing something rather interesting near the western ridge.
